strengths: Clear, well-motivated empirical observation (attention weight analysis) showing that VAR's next-scale attention concentrates on the immediately adjacent scale and on local spatial neighborhoods, which nicely motivates the proposed Markovian assumptions.

Significant practical efficiency gains are demonstrated: attention complexity reduced from O(N^2) to O(Nk), elimination of KV cache at inference, and up to 3-4x reduction in GPU memory, enabling training of a 310M model on 8 consumer RTX 4090 GPUs rather than high-end clusters.

Reasonably thorough ablation studies isolate the individual contributions of scale-Markov conditioning and spatial-Markov attention, and study the effect of the neighborhood size k and the number of preceding scales retained.
The method is evaluated in two practically relevant settings: training small models from scratch and fine-tuning larger pretrained VAR checkpoints, showing consistent efficiency benefits in both.
A theoretical complexity analysis (Appendix B) rigorously contrasts next-token O(N^3), vanilla next-scale O(N^2), and MVAR O(Nk) generation complexity.
weaknesses: The central quality claim -- that discarding almost all cross-scale conditioning and restricting attention to a small local neighborhood actually *improves* FID/IS over full-attention VAR -- is counter-intuitive and under-explained; the paper offers only a hand-wavy explanation ('focusing on more important information') rather than a rigorous analysis of why removing information should help rather than merely not hurt performance while saving compute. This raises questions about training budget parity or other confounds between MVAR and the VAR baselines used for comparison.

The attention-weight analysis used to justify the Markov assumptions is descriptive/observational rather than a rigorous test of conditional independence; concentrated attention weights do not necessarily imply that non-adjacent scale information is dispensable for optimal generation quality, especially at larger scales or higher resolutions.

All experiments are restricted to ImageNet 256×256 class-conditional generation; no evaluation at higher resolution or on text-to-image settings is provided, even though the claimed benefits (O(Nk) vs O(N^2)) should be most impactful precisely at higher resolutions/larger N, which is not empirically verified.

The core techniques (local/windowed attention akin to Swin/NAT-style neighborhood attention, and Markov-chain conditioning across a sequence) are individually well established in the literature; the novelty lies mainly in their combined application to the VAR next-scale framework rather than a fundamentally new modeling idea.

No direct quantitative comparison in the main results table against other efficient scale-wise or accelerated AR baselines (e.g., HART, Infinity, collaborative decoding, FastVAR) that are cited as related work, making it hard to judge whether MVAR's efficiency-quality trade-off is state-of-the-art relative to competing efficient VAR variants.

Some ablation and complexity details (e.g., the special treatment of the final two scales r9/r10 without causal masking accounting for 60% of tokens) are only briefly explained and could affect the fairness/clarity of the O(Nk) claims, since a large fraction of computation does not follow the strict Markov/local pattern discussed in the main text.

strengths: Provides a clear empirical motivation via attention-weight analysis (Fig. 2/3) showing that vanilla next-scale prediction exhibits strong locality across both scales and spatial positions, which nicely motivates the proposed simplifications.

The proposed scale-Markov trajectory and spatial-Markov (neighborhood) attention yield substantial and well-quantified efficiency gains: O(N^2)->O(Nk) attention complexity, elimination of KV cache, and roughly 3-4x reduction in memory footprint, enabling training on modest 8x RTX 4090 hardware.
Reasonably thorough ablations isolating the effect of the number of preceding scales in the conditioning prefix and the neighborhood size k, which help justify the chosen hyperparameters.
Reports both training-from-scratch (310M) and fine-tuning (600M/1B) settings, and shows that the approach can be applied to already pretrained VAR checkpoints for practical efficiency gains.
Includes a theoretical complexity derivation (Appendix B) that formalizes the claimed complexity reduction.
weaknesses: Core technical novelty is limited: spatial-Markov attention is essentially neighborhood/windowed local attention (already established, e.g., NATTEN, refs 13/14) applied to the VAR setting, and scale-Markov conditioning is simply truncating the autoregressive context to a single previous scale — both are fairly standard locality-exploiting tricks rather than a fundamentally new modeling contribution, despite being framed as a new 'Markovian' paradigm.

The claimed pure Markov design is undermined by an inconsistency revealed in Appendix A: the final two scales (accounting for 60% of tokens) disable causal masking and effectively still use denser attention/conditioning, contradicting the main narrative that MVAR strictly conditions on only the adjacent scale and neighborhood — this raises questions about how much of the reported efficiency gain genuinely stems from the proposed Markov assumption versus this exception.

Evaluation is restricted to ImageNet 256x256 class-conditional generation; there is no evaluation on higher resolutions, text-to-image, or video, which are precisely the settings where the claimed KV-cache-free/memory efficiency benefits would matter most (as acknowledged in the limitations section).

Performance improvements over VAR are quite marginal (FID 3.55->3.09, IS 280.4->285.5), and it is unclear whether the training schedules (e.g., 300 vs. VAR's reported 350 epochs) are strictly comparable, making it hard to attribute gains cleanly to the proposed method versus training differences.

No comparison against other recent efficient/accelerated VAR variants cited in related work (e.g., HART, Infinity, collaborative decoding, FastVAR) that address similar redundancy issues, despite these being natural and relevant baselines for the claimed efficiency contribution.

The paper is largely evaluated with FID/IS/Precision/Recall only; no human evaluation, diversity analysis, or higher-resolution/robustness tests are provided to substantiate the generation quality claims more broadly.
Substantial repetition of formulas, figures, and explanations between the main text and appendix reduces clarity and appears to pad the paper rather than add new insight.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated empirical analysis (attention-weight visualizations across scales and neighborhood sizes) that directly supports the two proposed Markov assumptions, making the design choices interpretable rather than purely heuristic.

Significant and well-quantified efficiency gains: reduces attention complexity from O(N^2) to O(Nk), eliminates the need for KV cache, and achieves up to 3.0-4.2x reduction in GPU memory, enabling training on modest hardware (8x RTX 4090) rather than large industrial clusters.

Comparable or slightly better generation quality (FID/IS/Precision/Recall) than the VAR baseline despite the reduced computational budget, evaluated both for models trained from scratch and for fine-tuned larger models (d16/d20/d24).

Reasonably thorough ablations isolating the effects of scale-Markov conditioning, spatial-Markov attention, number of preceding scales retained, and neighborhood size k, which support the paper's core claims.
Theoretical complexity analysis (Appendix B) formally contrasts next-token O(N^3), vanilla next-scale O(N^2), and MVAR O(Nk) complexities, adding rigor beyond purely empirical claims.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the core techniques (Markov/local conditioning across a sequence, and neighborhood-restricted attention akin to existing neighborhood attention transformers already cited) are individually well established; the contribution is largely their combination and application to VAR rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The justification for discarding non-adjacent scales and distant tokens is derived from analyzing the *already-trained* vanilla VAR's attention patterns, which is somewhat circular—since VAR was never incentivized to spread attention elsewhere, this does not rigorously establish that removing that capacity is truly information-preserving rather than a fortunate byproduct of the specific benchmark/architecture used.

Evaluation is restricted to ImageNet 256x256 class-conditional generation; there is no evaluation on higher resolutions, other datasets, or text-to-image settings, limiting evidence for generality of the proposed Markov assumptions.

Quantitative improvements over VAR in the main table are fairly modest (FID 3.55→3.09, IS 280.4→285.5), and the paper does not compare against other recent efficient VAR variants mentioned in related work (e.g., HART, Infinity, collaborative decoding, FastVAR) despite these being natural and relevant baselines.

Some reported numbers appear duplicated verbatim across tables (e.g., VAR-d16 FID/IS/Precision/Recall in Table 2 exactly match the 310M VAR row in Table 1), which raises questions about whether these are truly independent measurements or reused values, reducing confidence in the reported comparisons.

Limited exploration of failure modes or scenarios where the Markov assumptions might break down (e.g., globally coherent structures, long-range dependencies, complex multi-object scenes), leaving the generality of the approach only partially supported.

No wall-clock throughput/latency comparison is provided for the main results table (Table 1), making it harder to assess real inference speed benefits beyond the memory metric highlighted in Fig. 2(c) and Table 2.

strengths: Clear empirical motivation: attention weight analysis (Fig. 2, Fig. 3) across scales and neighborhood sizes provides concrete evidence for the scale- and spatial-redundancy claims that motivate the method.

Significant practical efficiency gains: reduces attention complexity from O(N^2) to O(Nk), eliminates KV cache at inference, and achieves 2.8-4.2x memory reduction, enabling training on 8 RTX 4090 GPUs rather than large GPU clusters.

Broad and fairly thorough experimental validation across multiple model scales (310M to 2B parameters), resolutions (256x256 and 512x512), and datasets (ImageNet, CelebA, FFHQ), plus both from-scratch training and fine-tuning of pretrained VAR checkpoints.

Useful ablation studies isolating the individual contributions of scale-Markov conditioning, spatial-Markov attention, neighborhood size k, number of preceding scales, and training ratio in the mixed training scheme.

Interesting and somewhat counter-intuitive finding that restricting conditioning/attention does not hurt and often improves FID/IS relative to the full-attention VAR baseline, supporting the redundancy hypothesis.
Reasonably good reproducibility support with detailed hyperparameters in the appendix and a stated intent to release code/checkpoints.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: the core techniques (windowed/neighborhood attention, Markov chain conditioning across a sequence) are direct adaptations of well-established ideas (e.g., Hassani et al.'s neighborhood attention, standard Markov assumptions) applied to the VAR framework, making the contribution primarily an engineering/efficiency exercise rather than a fundamentally new modeling idea.

Missing quantitative comparisons against other recent scale-wise/efficient AR baselines mentioned in related work (e.g., HART, Infinity, FlexVAR, collaborative decoding methods) that also target efficiency in next-scale prediction; only VAR is used as the primary baseline.

The surprising result that removing conditioning information consistently improves generation quality is not deeply analyzed or explained (e.g., via a regularization argument or theoretical grounding), leaving the mechanism behind the improvement somewhat unclear.

The attention-weight-based justification for the Markov assumptions could reflect an artifact of how the original VAR model was trained with full attention rather than true evidence that such redundancy is fundamental to the task; no causal/ablation analysis rules this out directly.

The mixed training strategy for the final two scales (r9, r10) relies on custom CUDA kernels and somewhat ad hoc scale-splitting heuristics, adding practical complexity that is under-explained in the main text and pushed to the appendix.

The pretrained-vs-fine-tuned comparison in Table 2 is not fully controlled (different training regimes/epochs for VAR vs MVAR), making it harder to cleanly attribute gains to the proposed method alone.
No human evaluation or more rigorous qualitative assessment beyond standard FID/IS/Precision/Recall metrics, which can sometimes be insensitive to certain visual artifacts.

Discussion of alternative efficient-attention paradigms outside of neighborhood attention (e.g., linear attention, sparse attention families) is largely absent, limiting positioning relative to the broader efficient-transformer literature.

strengths: The paper provides a clear empirical motivation via attention-weight analysis (Fig. 2, Fig. 3) showing that vanilla next-scale VAR models concentrate attention on the immediately preceding scale and on spatially local neighborhoods, which is an intuitive and reasonably well-illustrated observation.

The proposed scale-Markov trajectory and spatial-Markov attention yield substantial practical efficiency benefits: elimination of KV cache, reduced attention complexity from O(N^2) to O(Nk), and large empirical reductions in GPU memory (2.6x-4.2x) and training/inference time, which are valuable from a systems perspective.

The paper includes a reasonably extensive set of ablations (number of preceding scales, neighborhood size k, mixed training ratio) and additional experiments across multiple datasets (ImageNet-256, ImageNet-512, CelebA, FFHQ) and model scales (310M to 2B), showing some consistency of the efficiency/quality trade-off across settings.
A theoretical complexity analysis (Appendix A) is provided to formally support the claimed asymptotic complexity reduction compared to next-token and vanilla next-scale prediction.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the spatial-Markov attention is essentially a direct application of existing neighborhood/local attention mechanisms (Hassani & Shi, 2022; Hassani et al., 2023) to the VAR setting, and the scale-Markov truncation is a straightforward first-order Markov simplification; the paper does not offer substantial new algorithmic insight beyond combining known ideas for VAR.

The central large-scale ImageNet-256 comparison in Table 1 only reports a from-scratch model at the smallest scale (d16/310M); larger models (d20, d24) are only evaluated via fine-tuning pretrained VAR checkpoints (Table 2), so the claim of 'comparable or superior performance with large fine-tuned models' is not a fair test of whether the scale/spatial Markov assumptions hold when training larger models from scratch, which is the more scientifically relevant question and matches how the original VAR was trained.

The justification for the Markov assumptions rests solely on attention-weight magnitude analysis, which conflates attention weight concentration with functional necessity; high attention weight on the adjacent scale does not rigorously establish that non-adjacent scales are causally redundant, and no ablation isolates whether the observed gains stem from reduced redundancy versus other confounds (e.g., regularization effects of restricting context, different optimization dynamics).

Quality trade-offs are inconsistently reported: in Table 2, several fine-tuned MVAR variants show lower Recall than the VAR baselines (e.g., d16: 0.51→0.48, d20: 0.56→0.52, d24: 0.59→0.56), suggesting the efficiency gains may come at a precision/recall trade-off that is not adequately discussed or analyzed.

Missing comparisons to other efficient/accelerated VAR variants explicitly cited in the related work (e.g., HART, Infinity, FastVAR, collaborative decoding) that address similar redundancy/efficiency issues; without these baselines, it is hard to assess whether MVAR's efficiency-quality trade-off is actually competitive among existing efficient alternatives.

Experimental scale is modest relative to the field's standards for ImageNet-256 (largest reported FID numbers from scratch are only with a 310M model under a reduced 300-epoch schedule using modest batch size, and ablations use even shorter 50-epoch schedules), raising concerns about whether conclusions generalize to the compute/data regimes typically used in published next-scale AR literature.

Minor structural/writing issues such as an empty '3.1 Key Observations' subsection header with no content, suggesting insufficient polish, and some figures/tables are dense and not self-contained without extensive cross-referencing to the appendix.

strengths: Well-motivated empirical analysis (attention-weight visualizations across scales and neighborhood sizes) that clearly justifies the design choices before introducing the method.

Substantial and consistently demonstrated efficiency gains: ~2.8-3.2x memory reduction, elimination of KV cache, and reduced GFLOPs/wall-clock time across multiple model sizes (310M-2B) and resolutions (256x256, 512x512).

Comprehensive experimental validation across several datasets (ImageNet, CelebA, FFHQ) and settings (from-scratch training and fine-tuning of pretrained VAR checkpoints), which strengthens generalizability claims.
Thorough ablation studies covering number of preceding scales, spatial neighborhood size k, and mixed-training ratio, providing good insight into design sensitivity.
The method enables training with modest hardware (8 RTX 4090 GPUs), which improves accessibility/reproducibility for a compute-constrained community.

Counterintuitive but interesting result that restricting conditioning can match or slightly improve generation quality (FID/IS) relative to the dense VAR baseline, suggesting redundant conditioning may not only be wasteful but potentially harmful.
Clear theoretical complexity derivation (O(N^2) to O(Nk)) supporting the practical speed/memory measurements.
weaknesses: Core technical ingredients (localized/neighborhood attention via dilated neighborhood attention kernels, Markov-chain conditioning) are adopted from existing prior work (Hassani & Shi, 2022; Hassani et al., 2023) rather than newly proposed, making the technical novelty somewhat incremental — the main contribution is the application/combination to the next-scale VAR paradigm.

The explanation for why removing scale/spatial context improves quality is under-analyzed; the paper relies mainly on empirical attention-weight correlations without deeper theoretical or causal analysis of why less conditioning helps rather than hurts.

Limited comparison against other efficient VAR variants explicitly discussed in related work (e.g., HART, Infinity, collaborative decoding) — Table 1 and Table 2 comparisons are essentially only against vanilla VAR, missing broader positioning against contemporaneous efficient autoregressive image generators.
No reported variance/error bars across multiple runs/seeds for FID/IS, so some reported improvements (e.g., 0.1-0.5 FID gains) may fall within normal run-to-run variability.

Experiments are capped at 512x512 resolution and largest reported scale is 2B parameters trained only on the relatively simple CelebA dataset; it remains unclear whether the Markov assumptions hold as well for more complex/high-resolution or text-conditioned generation.

The attention-weight visualizations used to motivate the Markov assumptions come from a model that was itself trained with dense attention, so the observed locality could partly be an artifact of training dynamics rather than intrinsic properties of the data distribution — the ablations partially address this but a more rigorous justification would strengthen the claims.
Minor structural/clarity issues, such as an empty 'Key observations' subsection header (3.1) with content deferred until 3.2, and some redundancy across figures/tables in the appendix.
